analysis.one_liner: Eliminates the requirement that federal construction projects pay workers the local prevailing wage.
analysis.headline: The bill died without a vote, never leaving the House committee it was assigned to.
analysis.plain_summary: The Davis-Bacon Act, on the books since 1931, requires companies doing federally financed construction to pay workers the locally prevailing wage — roughly, the rate skilled workers in that area normally earn. The Copeland Act requires Labor Department rules on contractors' payroll reporting. This bill would repeal both laws, letting contractors on federal projects pay whatever wages they choose. It was introduced by Rep. Ron Paul with 3 Republican cosponsors, referred to the House Education and the Workforce Committee, then to a subcommittee, and never advanced further.
analysis.who_benefits: Government construction contractors and subcontractors would gain the most, because wages are usually their largest cost on federal projects, and the prevailing wage floor is what keeps those costs up. Taxpayers would bear some savings on the bid side of federal construction contracts — the savings come directly out of workers' paychecks.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the Davis-Bacon Act, which requires locally prevailing wages for laborers and mechanics on federally financed construction of public buildings and public works [S2][S3].
Repeals the Copeland Act, which requires the Labor Secretary to regulate contractors and subcontractors on such projects [S2][S3].
The repeal would take effect 30 days after enactment but would not affect contracts already in existence or bids already outstanding [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Construction workers on federal projects — the people the prevailing wage rules exist to protect — would see their pay drop to whatever the contractor decides, since federal contracts would no longer carry a wage floor. Workers and communities surrounding federal projects would feel it too, because the prevailing wage standard holds up pay rates in the local construction market.

drawbacks.text: Repealing Davis-Bacon removes the only wage floor on federally funded construction, likely cutting pay for the laborers and mechanics the law covers and pressuring wages in the local construction market generally [S2].

The strongest argument for the bill — and its honest cost to acknowledge — is that prevailing wage requirements raise the cost of federal construction for taxpayers; the trade-off is that those savings come straight out of construction workers' wages.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Any taxpayer savings from lower bids on federal construction would be paid for by reduced wages for the workers building those projects, and a smaller share of the construction dollar going to skilled trades could erode the trained workforce that public projects depend on. The benefit is diffuse and speculative; the cost is concentrated and direct.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Education and the Workforce Committee and then to a subcommittee, where it sat until the Congress ended without ever coming up for a vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Ron Paul introduced the bill on October 23, 1997, with 3 Republican cosponsors [S1][S4].
The House referred it to the Committee on Education and the Workforce the day it was introduced [S1][S5].
Two weeks later it was referred to the Subcommittee on Workforce Protections, where it remained with no further action for the rest of the 105th Congress [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Construction workers on federally funded projects are better off, because the prevailing wage floor they rely on stays in place. Federal construction contractors lose nothing they already had.

for.name: Rep. Ron Paul
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the Davis-Bacon and Copeland Acts.

against.name: House Committee on Education and the Workforce
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to a subcommittee and never scheduled a markup or a vote.

sides.party_line_note: All four sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans; the bill made no progress in the Republican-run House committee and drew no Democratic support.

industries.note: Repeal would let contractors on federal projects pay below the local prevailing wage, cutting their largest cost — labor — at the direct expense of their workers.
Davis-Bacon is the wage floor for construction workers on federal jobs; its repeal would directly cut their pay and put downward pressure on local construction wages.
